## The Museum of Almost

The Museum of Almost occupies the second floor of a building between a locksmith and a bakery that opens at four. There is no sign above the stairs, only a blue door with a brass handle polished by many nervous hands.

Admission costs one memory you are willing to leave behind.

I went on a wet Thursday, carrying an umbrella I had forgotten to open. The attendant was a small woman in a green coat, though the weather had been warm for weeks. She examined my ticket—a conversation I had never had with my brother—then held the door.

“You chose carefully,” she said. “Most people bring something they would rather forget.”

The first room contained a staircase painted onto the wall. At its top was a door, closed and glowing faintly beneath the peeling wallpaper.

“Opportunity,” said a label. “Recoverable until the moment you begin explaining it.”

In a glass case nearby lay a letter, addressed but never posted. Its contents changed when I looked away. A recording played beside it, a woman rehearsing an apology that had never happened:

“You don’t have to make it smaller,” she said. “You only have to let me understand it.”

I moved on.

There was a field of yellow flowers behind the ticket desk, although the ceiling had not been removed. A railway timetable listed destinations in a city that burned down before I was born. A child’s coat hung from a hook, and beneath it stood a pair of grown-up shoes. A bell rang somewhere out of sight, followed by applause.

At the end of the corridor, the attendant was waiting.

“Most people search for the life they should have had,” she said. “It’s easy to find. We keep several.”

“What do you keep here, then?”

“Mostly what they nearly had.”

We passed a case containing an entire Wednesday afternoon. Nothing appeared to be happening inside it. A cup of tea stood on a windowsill, steam curling without cooling. Somewhere, a radio played. Dust turned slowly in a stripe of sun.

“I don’t remember that,” I said.

“You don’t have to.” She drew a small key from her coat. “The museum only opens for the things people are willing to miss.”

I almost asked her about the ticket I had given at the door. The conversation I had never had. The brother who had become polite in our arguments, and distant in our silences. I had rehearsed it for years.

The key lay in her palm.

I remembered then that a memory is not a box. It is a road. What we lose, we do not lose all at once. We lose the turnings, the weather, the exact quality of light on the day. And sometimes, if we are fortunate, we discover that the road has not vanished. Only our certainty about where it leads.

I left the key on the table.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The blue door stood open behind me, though I could not see anyone returning my ticket.

The walk home took longer than usual. I had no particular reason to take the long way.

But I did.
